'''Don R. Swanson''' (October 10, 1924 – November 18, 2012) was an American information scientist, most known for his work in [[literature-based discovery]] in the biomedical domain. His particular method has been used as a model for further work, and is often referred to as [[Swanson linking]]. He was an investigator in the [[Arrowsmith System]] project,<ref>{{cite web|author=Vetle Torvik |url=http://arrowsmith.psych.uic.edu/arrowsmith_uic/index.html |title=The Arrowsmith Project Homepage |publisher=Arrowsmith.psych.uic.edu |date=2007-12-20 |access-date=2012-12-13}}</ref> which seeks to determine meaningful links between [[MEDLINE|Medline]] articles to identify previously undiscovered public knowledge. He had been professor emeritus of the [[University of Chicago]] since 1996, and remained active in a post-retirement appointment until his health began to decline in 2009.

==Life==
Swanson was born in [[Los Angeles]] on October 10, 1924, the son of Harry Windfield and Grace Clara (Sandstrom) Swanson. He served with the [[United States Navy Reserve]] from 1943 to 1946,<ref name=WWA>{{cite book | title=Who's Who in America | publisher=Marquis Who's Who LLC | year=2007 | page=4483 | isbn=978-0-8379-6999-2 | url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_0837969999_2/page/4438/mode/2up?q=swanson }}</ref> and received his B.S. in physics at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]], [[Pasadena, California]] in 1945. He gained his M.A from [[Rice University|Rice Institute]], [[Houston, Texas]], two years later, and then a PhD in Theoretical Physics from the [[University of California at Berkeley]] in 1952.<ref name=UChicagoNews>{{cite web | first=Susie | last=Allen | title=Don R. Swanson, information science pioneer, 1924–2012 | website=UChicago News | url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/don-r-swanson-information-science-pioneer-1924-2012 | date=December 6, 2012 }}</ref>

From 1952 to 1954 Swanson worked as a computer systems analyst at [[Hughes Aircraft Company]] Research and Development Laboratories in [[Culver City, California]]. In 1955 had joined [[Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation]].<ref name=WWA/> Initially working as a research scientist,<ref>{{cite book | author=An Introduction to Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation | title=An Introduction to Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation | year=1956 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hAlSAQAAMAAJ&q=%22don+r.+swanson%22}}</ref> by 1959 he was manager of the Synthetic Intelligence Dept. at Ramo-Wooldridge. There he led a project contracted to the [[Council on Library Resources]], with [[Noam Chomsky]] and Paul L. Garvin as linguistic advisors, to investigate [[machine indexing]] of 'a small experimental library of scientific text (ca. 300,000 words)'.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Mechanical Indexing and Retrieval to be Investigated | journal=Science Information News | volume=1 | issue=5 | date=October–November 1959 | page=5 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NUMLYi_vFpQC&pg=PT8 }}</ref> Swanson collaborated further with Garvin on Russian-English [[machine translation]], considering problems of [[polysemy]], in work funded by the [[Rome Air Development Center]].

In December 1959 he attended the annual meeting of the [[American Anthropological Association]], speaking on 'Engineering Aspects' in a symposium on the uses of data processing equipment in anthropology.<ref>{{cite book | author=American Anthropological Association | title=Program of the American Anthropological Association Annual Meeting | year=1959 | url=}}</ref> By 1961 he was a member of the [[National Science Foundation]]'s Science Information Council.<ref>{{cite report | author=National Science Foundation | title= 11th Annual Report, 1961 | page=164 | year=1962 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DF_KQTo9kBkC&pg=PA164}}</ref>

In 1963 Swanson joined the [[University of Chicago]] as a professor in the [[University of Chicago Graduate Library School|Graduate School of Library Science]]. He also served as dean of the graduate school from 1963 to 1972, from 1977 to 1979 and again from 1987 to 1989. From 1972 to 1976 he was a research fellow at the [[Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis]].<ref name=WWA/>

In the 1980s Swanson pioneered [[literature-based discovery]] in the biomedical domain, building the [[Arrowsmith System]] around a discovery method that has since become known as [[Swanson linking]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Smalheiser |first=Neil R. |date=2017-12-01 |title=Rediscovering Don Swanson:The Past, Present and Future of Literature-based Discovery |journal=Journal of Data and Information Science |language=en |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=43–64 |doi=10.1515/jdis-2017-0019 |pmc=5771422 |pmid=29355246}}</ref>  He hypothesized that the combination of two separately published results indicating an A-B relationship and a B-C relationship are evidence of an unknown or unexplored A-C relationship. He used this to propose [[fish oil]] as a treatment for [[Raynaud syndrome]], due to their shared relationship with [[blood viscosity]].<ref name="Swanson 1986 7–18">{{Cite journal |last=Swanson |first=Don R. |date=1986 |title=Fish Oil, Raynaud's Syndrome, and Undiscovered Public Knowledge |journal=Perspectives in Biology and Medicine |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=7–18 |doi=10.1353/pbm.1986.0087 |pmid=3797213 |s2cid=33675760 |issn=1529-8795}}</ref>

From 1992 to 1996 Swanson was professor of the biosciences collection division and the humanities division at Chicago. In 1996 he became professor emeritus.<ref name=WWA/>

In 2000, Swanson was awarded the [[Award of Merit - Association for Information Science and Technology]], the highest honor of the society, for his "lifetime achievements in research and scholarship."<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.asis.org/Bulletin/Dec-01/inside_asist.html |title=Inside ASIST<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2007-02-02 |archive-date=2016-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084534/http://www.asis.org/Bulletin/Dec-01/inside_asist.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>Swanson, Don Richard. 2001. “ASIST Award of Merit Acceptance Speech on the Fragmentation of Knowledge, the Connection Explosion, and Assembling Other People’s Ideas.” ''Bulletin of the American Society for Information Science & Technology'' 27 (3): 12–14.</ref>
